newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia details 1997 economic policy draft.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia details 1997 economic policy draft.

text.p: Yugoslavia said on Monday it would aim at price and dinar stability in 1997 while promoting industrial and export growth.

Deputy Prime Minister Jovan Zebic, presenting an official policy draft at an economics seminar, said the dinar's exchange rate would remain fixed at 3.3 to the German mark despite market fears of devaluation.

"Our top priority is to maintain price and dinar stability...that will in turn contribute to intensifying structural changes and privatisation and give impetus to more vigorous economic activity," he said.
"We want...very dynamic growth in a stable environment although we know it will be difficult to achieve."

Yugoslavia needs substantial foreign investment but recognises that money will start flowing only after ties with international financial institutions and the World Trade Organisation are restored, Zebic said.
Despite a vague commitment to privatise the inefficient state sector, the government has rejected wide privatisation, claiming it would lead to a further decline in gross domestic product (GDP).

"The loss would be equivalent to what we experienced during sanctions. We cannot allow another drop in GDP. Therefore, we decided on a longer privatisation that will help increase our GDP," Zebic said.
The government also needs to restore public confidence in the banking system to encourage savings that could be used to finance production.

GDP is slated to rise 13 percent in 1997, with growth in industry of 14 percent, agriculture 6 percent, construction 12 percent, transport 16.5 percent, trade 16 per cent, catering 20 percent and other sectors around 15 percent.
Public spending will account for 47.5 percent of GDP, while average wages and pensions will rise by 12 percent.
Zebic said the unchanged exchange rate would "stimulate exports and contribute to an even greater hard currency inflow needed for bigger industrial output."

The central bank's discount rate will remain positive in real terms, while commercial lending rates will be set freely, based on supply and demand on the financial market, the government said in its economic policy paper.
Zebic said the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) will strengthen its control function to produce stricter financial discipline.

"The NBY will regulate liquidity of the banking sector through selling and buying securities on the market with neutral monetary effect," Zebic said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
